title: What a verb decides
ask: Pick what the question is about

items.q: Which of these is the dictionary form (bezokolicznik) of the verb meaning "to write"?
items.why: pisać is the infinitive — the form you look up and learn. The others are used forms: pisanie-type forms are nouns, piszę is "I write", pisałem is "I wrote", pisze is "he writes".

items.q: How many tenses does Polish have?
items.why: Present, past and future. English has more shapes (I write, I am writing, I have written, I will have been writing), but Polish puts most of that meaning into aspect, not into extra tenses.

items.q: Which of these tells you the aspect of a verb?
opts: Its ending in the dictionary form
Whether the dictionary marks it impf or pf
The tense it is used in
items.a: Whether the dictionary marks it impf or pf
items.why: Aspect is a property of the verb itself, not of the sentence: every verb is either imperfective or perfective, and a dictionary says which with impf/pf or ndk./dk. The infinitive ending hints at the family it belongs to, but it does not decide aspect.

items.q: You look up "buy" and find kupić. What should you write down?
items.why: Learn both halves of the pair as one item. kupować is the process, kupić is the finished act. Learning one half is the most common way to learn a verb wrong — chapter 2 is entirely about this.

items.q: In a Polish past-tense form like pisałem, what does the ending show that English "I wrote" does not?
items.why: pisałem (male speaker) versus pisałam (female speaker). Polish past-tense forms carry gender, so the speaker's sex is never hidden.

items.q: Which ending is not a possible Polish infinitive ending?
items.why: -ć (pisać), -c (móc) and -ść (iść) all occur. -æ is not a Polish letter or ending at all.

title: Reading the infinitive
ask: What family does the ending point to?

items.q: czytać ends in -ać. What is its present tense likely to look like?
items.why: The -ać family overwhelmingly goes to -am, -asz: czytać → czytam, mieszkać → mieszkam, pytać → pytam. It is the largest family in the language.

items.q: mówić ends in -ić. What is its present tense likely to look like?
items.why: The -ić family goes to -ię, -isz: mówić → mówię, mówisz; robić → robię, robisz; dzwonić → dzwonię, dzwonisz.

items.q: Which of these verbs is perfective?
items.why: napisać is perfective — the finished act of writing. pisać and czytać are imperfective. piec means "to bake" and is imperfective too.

items.q: Which of these is a legitimate way to translate szukać?
items.why: szukać is to look for, an ongoing search, and it takes the genitive. To find is znaleźć, its perfective partner — a different word, and that difference matters (chapter 2).

items.q: A verb marked pf in a dictionary has:
items.why: A perfective verb describes a completed act, and something already complete cannot be happening now. Its present-looking forms are the future: napisać → napiszę = "I will write".

items.q: Write the infinitive of "to be".
items.why: być — the most irregular verb in the language, and the one you cannot avoid (chapter 8).

items.q: Write the infinitive of "to have".
items.why: mieć — a -m, -sz verb: mam, masz, ma, mamy, macie, mają.

title: Transitive or not?
ask: Does it take a direct object?

items.q: Czytam ___ — "I am reading a book". Which case is book in?
items.why: czytać is transitive and takes a plain direct object: the accusative. Czytam książkę. Note that a negation would turn it genitive: Nie czytam książki.

items.q: Szukam ___ — "I am looking for the keys". Which case?
items.why: szukać takes the genitive even though English "look for" takes a plain object. The case is a property of the verb, not of the English translation — this is rekcja, chapter 9.

items.q: Pomagam ___ — "I am helping my mum". Which case?
items.why: pomagać takes the dative: Pomagam mamie. The person helped is the receiver of the help, and the receiver is the dative's job.

items.q: Which sentence is correct?
items.why: The object of mieć is accusative (bilet), but negating a verb turns that object into the genitive: nie mam biletu. This rule is so reliable that Polish teachers call it the negation genitive.

items.q: Which is the better translation of Znam Łódź.?
items.why: znać = to know a person, a place or a language — familiarity. wiedzieć = to know a fact. You znasz Łódź but wiesz, where the station is.

items.q: Which of these verbs is intransitive?
items.why: iść (to go on foot) takes no direct object; it takes a destination with a preposition: Idę do sklepu (do + genitive), Idę na koncert (na + accusative).

items.q: Someone says Kupuję chleb when they mean "I'll buy the bread (now, once)". What went wrong?
opts: They used the imperfective where the perfective is meant
items.a: They used the imperfective where the perfective is meant
items.why: For a single, completed purchase you want the perfective kupię: Kupię chleb. Kupuję describes a process or a habit — "I buy bread (regularly)" or "I'm in the middle of buying it". The case was fine; the aspect was not.

items.q: Why does Ja to zrobię sound different from To zrobię?
opts: The pronoun adds emphasis — "it's me who'll do it"
items.a: The pronoun adds emphasis — "it's me who'll do it"
items.why: Polish endings already say who does it, so an added pronoun is a choice: it stresses the person. To zrobię is neutral; ja to zrobię says "I'll do it, not you".

items.q: Someone wants to say "I am writing" using napisać. Why can't they?
opts: napisać is perfective and has no present tense
items.a: napisać is perfective and has no present tense
items.why: A completed act cannot be happening now. napiszę is the future: "I will write (and it will be written)". For "I am writing", use the imperfective: piszę.

items.q: What is the difference between Piszę list and Napiszę list?
items.why: Piszę — I am writing / I write, the process. Napiszę — I will write it and it will be done, the result. The same root, the same object, a different claim about completion.
